text: What exactly do you mean by "sudden-onset symptoms," and how would you describe the sensation of vertigo? Has this been accompanied by hearing loss, tinnitus, or any difficulty speaking?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the detailed description; the brief duration is a crucial clue. Have you experienced any weakness, numbness, double vision, or trouble swallowing during those episodes? Also, could you clarify if you noticed any changes in your hearing or balance before you went to bed?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Audiogram and MRI Brain (internal auditory canal). REQUEST IMAGES: Please return the MRI sequences immediately. While we await those results, have you recently had any new head trauma or severe headaches?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Audiometry: Within normal limits for age. Head Imaging (MRI): Normal, with no evidence of stroke or masses. Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient's symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back. Vital Signs: Temperature 97.7°F (36.5°C), Blood Pressure 134/85 mmHg, Heart Rate 85 bpm, Respiratory Rate 13 breaths/min, Oxygen Saturation 98% on room air. General Examination: Appearance is a healthy man with a normal gait; Neurological exam shows physiologic nystagmus observed, with severe symptoms and notable nystagmus when head is turned to the left and laid back; Cranial Nerve Exam is unremarkable.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Gastroenteritis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

While Gastroenteritis explains nausea and vomiting, it does not cause true rotational vertigo lasting only 3 minutes without fever or diarrhea; furthermore, your denial of headaches and neurological deficits makes stroke or acoustic neuroma less likely. The brevity of the episode and lack of other symptoms point strongly to displaced otoconia in the inner ear. Would you like me to proceed with a Dix-Hallpike maneuver to confirm this?
